This is the first time I've ever written a review for a game, but this one deserved it. I'm not a hardcore, or professional reviewer, but bear with me. 

This game, to me, was a masterpiece. The first few levels will have you still getting used to the controls, struggling a little to fight off the enemies, but once you get the basics down, it'll be a joyride for the first few levels. The game progressively gets harder, though. The higher you go, the harder it gets. Some of the encounters with even the normal enemies are seemingly difficult, and might take you multiple deaths to figure out. Maybe more. Some levels seemed like a cakewalk to me, while others took me tens of deaths to beat. It really forces you to implement all of the abilities you unlock if you want to make your life easier. 

The difficulty of the game might be a turn off for some, but it's that type of difficulty that will keep you coming back. Every time you die multiple times in a row, and feel like punching your desk, it makes you want to come back so you can finally finish that mission. It's so satisfying when you finally beat the encounter that you were stuck on, and same with the boss fights. 

The story of the game was nice, and the characters were understandable. Each had a set goal in mind, and were determined to reach it. While it may not be the best story line, maybe even cliche, it wasn't terrible. The combat totally makes up for this, though. It was so satisfying to see the heads of your enemies get chopped cleanly off, or their bodies split into two. The game truly is beautiful when it comes to this, and I think they got the combat down perfectly for a game of this type.

I would describe Ghostrunner as Titanfall and Dishonored having a surrogate baby with Mirror's Edge (while Cyberpunk 2077 is claiming to be the father). Yeah, that. This is one of the best games I've played in a while and I have a lot of good things to say. For players that are new to FPS action games (such as the mentioned above) or new to gaming in general. I must warn that this is a HARDCORE game. If you are not good, you will die a lot and that's a fact. I highly recommend that you play at least one of the games mentioned above to easily be comfortable with Ghostrunner. Heck, even Call of Duty: Black Ops III will help you which plays loosely like Titanfall.

+ Ghostrunner's gameplay is solid, I can say a lot about it but it would take up this whole guide. Combat-wise, it is simple as hack-and-slash. However, Ghostrunner offers good enemy variety to attack which should change the way you play. It's a one hit kill for all enemies, however to sort of balance it you are also a one hit kill to anyone. Additionally, the skills that are unlocked upon playing the game are insanely good, especially Tempest and Blink. Movement-wise, the game offers a fast-paced Titanfall-Dishonored experience with sliding, wallrunning, teleporting, grappling and so on. All of these feel fluid and satisfying to chain. For a person like me, I quickly attached to the movement, and so I began my journey speedrunning the levels. God, speedrunning is insane but it's so good to see. People will instantly be lost to the way you play if you know your sh*t. Level design is also good, depending on how fast you play the levels can be very short. 

+ Graphics-wise, Ghostrunner is beautiful. It perfectly captures the Japanese cyberpunk theme (probably better than CP2077 itself) and much of my liking is with the lighting. Performance shouldn't be a problem as my setup is capable of running 144+ fps on 4K ultra (without DLSS). You seriously have to appreciate the great optimization from Unreal Engine 4. And with DLSS enabled, the insane frames per second gives you buttery smooth gameplay. Props to the devs for DLSS and ray-tracing support. After a few patches the game is in a much stable state and I receive much less crashes, and ray-tracing is much more optimized. Now don't get me wrong, ray-tracing looks great especially reflections but regardless the base lighting is already great, and the difference with RTX on from off is minimal in my opinion, and a game that is fast-paced you won't have time to notice the change in lighting. A minor but preferred feature that is not in the game is the ability to see your POV, it kinda feels like you're floating sometimes without feet.

+ Surprisingly, Ghostrunner has a decent story. The story is told throughout the levels you play and I do seem to have a connection with the characters despite only being dialogue. It's also good to hear some dry humor between the Ghostrunner and the Architect. Depending on how fast you play, the story is short at around 5-6 hours of gameplay. However, there is support for New Game + with Hardcore mode, and it is no joke when they say it's hardcore.

+ The soundtrack. Wow, no words can describe how badass it is. Similarly to Doom, without the soundtrack it still plays great. But with the soundtrack, it's legendary. Also like with Mirror's Edge, (almost) every level has its unique soundtrack which makes every level memorable. Huge props to the composer. 

+ Finally, Post-launch DLC. For the most part, new gameplay additions are free which is always good to hear. Hardcore is included as post-launch, I'll take any form of NG+ to add to my time. Kill Run mode is a good addition, though lacks true replayability. I wish they added at least 10 levels at launch, or if they planned to add more in the future. Photo Mode is a godsend in any game, but with a graphically stunning game like Ghostrunner it is wallpaper free real estate. Wave mode is also a neat gamemode to really show off your gameplay skills, pretty fun to speedrun as well. The rest of the paid DLC are cosmetic only, and they look good enough to satisfy me

Project Hel is its separate expansion from vanilla Ghostrunner, and plays partly different to the original. Gameplay for Hel took a little getting used to due to the new mechanics like the jump, but it offers a different experience to the original which I seemed to have enjoyed. But I must say, Hel's movement is inferior to the original. New enemies are present in Project Hel, however the don't necessarily feel like a threat compared to enemies like Mechs and Wardens which are also present in this expansion. If you were enticed to Ghostrunner's story, Project Hel offers the backstory of the events during the game, and answers most questions of how it came to be. Which to say, the story is also well-presented despite it being presented through dialogue. I'm a little saddened there are only 6 levels in this DLC, I would have been satisfied with a minimum of 8 for this DLC. But to be fair, the levels are a little longer than the original Ghostrunner. Nonetheless, more levels means more soundtracks which is always a win.


+ My main request to make this game better is proper mod support, mainly custom maps and gameplay changes. The community may be small, but it's strong. I'd be delighted to follow any custom made mods for Ghostrunner.

Here's my summary:

+ Great gameplay, phenomenal for speedrunning
+ Excellent graphics, performance and (base) optimization
+ Decent story, can play with different difficulties
+ Awesome soundtrack
+ Free DLC modes, cheap DLC skins
+ Sells for okay price, best buy on sale

- Gameplay geared for hardcore players
- Poor optimization with ray-tracing, but has been fixed
- Lack of mod support
- Minor performance issues, but has been mostly fixed

Overall, Ghostrunner is an excellent game, for me at least. Some people are put off by the immense amount of restarting (which is why I said it is a HARDCORE game). But nonetheless, I will support the game by buying their cosmetics. I am very intrigued in the next Ghostrunner game!

[i]Ghostrunner[/i] is a first-person cyberpunk action game taking place in a post-apocalyptic world built by a mysterious architect where the surviving humans live. The player is responsible for saving the remainders of humanity by running on walls, using superhuman powers, and slicing down enemies.

The game can be a bit difficult for most players. It is a one-hit game where every character dies on a single hit, including the player. Luckily, there are a good number of checkpoints throughout the game. These checkpoints help players keep going from a point they would not regret dying, but they do not work as a save point. It is not possible to save the game in the middle of a level.

Although the combat can sometimes be quite frustrating, both the platforming and combat experiences are super fun and satisfying. The game features cyberspace sections where there is either collecting, platforming, puzzle-solving, or a tutorial introducing a new ability. These sections allow players to slow down and relax a bit in such a fast-paced game. The narration mostly happens in the background as the player plays the game, and it does not interrupt the gameplay.

The visuals are impressive in both physical and cyberspace worlds, but it is the music that needs special attention. Without the well-composed music, the game would not be this much fun and satisfying. The music makes everything better in this game. It makes the player feel like a true cyber ninja.

Even though the game is relatively short, new modes are constantly being added to the game. The difficulty of the game makes it hard to be playable by everyone. Players who can easily get annoyed for dying hundreds of times and potentially give up after a while may prefer avoiding this game. It is highly recommended for anyone looking for a challenge or who enjoys fast-paced sword combat and parkour games.

Let me just get something out of the way.

The writing is ass. It's predictable, it's lame, it takes itself seriously to a borderline offensive degree. It's exactly what you would expect from videogame writing, with all the horrible implications that phrase entails.

That being said, if bland stories and pained exposition usually don't bother you, they won't bother you here either. It's not especially egregious, just bad.

And you're not here for that anyways, you're here for a fast-paced skinnerbox that keeps outputting cool shit in return for your time. 
And that's something this game is pretty good at.

It's got its problems, quite a few actually, raytracing doesn't seem to make use of RTX cards, or at least not efficiently, and you may have to override High DPI scaling behavior for the game, or it might just ignore mouse inputs at random intervals, which is seriously annoying in a game that often requires super precise timings. Your grappling hook feels 'off' somehow, your slow-motion move is often necessary, but honestly feels like it breaks the flow of the game.

BUT:

Damn, you get to run around real fast and kill dudes in one hit. There are some interesting choices in the level and enemy design, from a gameplay perspective, and while you'll be blowing through all the content relatively quick, those will keep them interesting during replays, especially if you're trying to outperform your friends, their times and deaths for stages will be visible at the end of a run, a great way to let players motivate themselves without giving them explicit goals, which can often cause burnout.

And all the while the soundtrack just keeps egging you on, pushing you to go a little faster, to play a little more recklessly...

The game's short-ish runtime is pretty easily justified by its replayability and cost. It's no masterpiece, but if the trailer looks fun to you, I guarantee it will be a lot of fun to play.

A cyberpunk game that doesn’t suck, the combat is the real shine here with the challenge it brings along with some parkour sprinkled in to make it fun to be badass while being in the sub-genre of one hit kill games will turn off a lot non-masochists. The only thing that brings it down from being great are the weird and pointless virtual sections, parkour jank with wall running and 2/3 bosses being average. I would love to see a sequel that would address these issues and easily bring this to a staple game like the ones I recommend below.

 [h1]More in depth: [/h1]
[list]
    [*]The STORY is half told while you are traversing which never breaks the flow of the game; it seems like here the developers know what kind of player will be playing the game, but it’s impossible to pay attention as you’re playing the game, so I don’t know what the game was about. Then there are these inside the MATRIX SECTIONS SPRINKLED THAT BRING THE GAME TO A CRAWL AS YOU SLOWLY WALK without any dashing with exposition dump and teach new abilities sometimes. These sections are the weakest part as it hurts the pacing and could at least let me use my parkour. The platforming is braindead and has weird collect orbs to progress, it’s like this section was made by a separate studio and just randomly put in this game. It’s about 1-2 hours of the whole game so 25% of the game is boring, easy and pointless.

    [*]    The COMBAT HERE IS THE TRUE GEM as it feels like you have a lot of ways to kill the enemy in some sections in any order you want with whatever ability and perks you have. The perks are really nice here as you have limited area to fit these tetris pieces in that have meaningful impact on how you want to focus your playstyle, more dash and defense heavy, upgrade your skills to reach farther, recharge or use multiple times per charge. I did rarely use the skills though, as it never felt necessary, but maybe that’s my playstyle to just use the sword. The enemy total variety is low when compared to some others, but the attacks and placement in every single encounter felt unique and with the parkour thrown into said encounters never felt dull or repetitive, even when dying 30 times at most in some areas. This is also what I wanted the combat for Cyberpunk 2077 to feel like.

   [*]    INSTANT RESTARTS SHOULD BE TURNED ON, having a button decided to instantly start over before anything bad happens saves a lot of time but can sometimes be cheesed to prevent deaths. Without this, the game would be more annoying for sure.

   [*]    The WORLD IS NICE to look at and even with a lot of parkour thrown in, it for the most part feels like an actual place instead of clearly marked follow the path stuff. You know in games where the look of the world can be brought down by gamifying the elements to help you traverse the world, here it doesn’t feel like that. The music thrown in is really fun to get into the flow while you traverse both combat and platforming arenas with a grapple hook because every game needs one if it wants to be fast and fluid. YOU CAN UNLOCK COOL NEW SWORD SKINS BY EXPLORING, EVEN THOUGH THE GAME IS LINEAR. There are other audio logs and items that flesh out the story and world, but they weren’t really worth it for me.

   [*]    There are 3 BOSSES, the first 2 are good with the better one being the laser tower grapple parkour spiral of death and wasn’t as hard as some people make it out to be, but it is a huge spike in challenge as you are not prepared for it at all, but you get a lot of checkpoints. The other one is a duel with a robot lady that you have to time your parries and do it all in one life, so the challenge was there, but it didn’t feel like a sword fight like Sekiro or Jedi Knight and was weaker for it. The final boss felt like a standard generic boss as you wait for the weirdly slow dr octopus swings, and do a little parkour, but it didn’t feel like what I expect from a boss fight. The true final boss is the parkour in the virtual matrix afterwards. 

   [*]    THE FINAL LEVEL IS THE BIGGEST SPIKE IN CHALLENGE and it shows how bad the parkour really is or me. I don’t know how sometimes I wall run flawlessly and then other 10 times I fall to my death because of something I can’t figure out. It feels like wind is pushing me back and down. I would have loved to see one huge arena or stages of arenas to push the limit of the player in the other more interesting aspect of the game, partly because I suck more than most at platforming. This game pushed my limit and patience at times. It also did end so quick, right as the flow gets good I just wanted more

[h1] Ghostrunner is a fast-paced first-person action game where the player has to slash through dozens of enemies in order to survive in a cruel world and find all the needed answers.  [/h1] 

[b] Pros: [/b]

+Outstanding level design
+ Fast-paced action gameplay 
+ Amazing synth-wave soundtrack 
+ Pretty impressive visuals 
+ Challenging and interesting gameplay
+ “Just one more try” feeling

[b] Cons: [/b]

- Ray tracing feature is simply not functional 
- The difficulty curve is weird sometimes
- The game can be a bit annoying on certain levels 
- Dull and unremarkable bosses 
- A bit shallow story with a VERY predictable ending

Ghostrunner was one of those games I was not waiting for at all. I heard about it a few times and it didn’t interest me that much, it looked a bit weird and not that impressive for me. Once it was released, I saw a bunch of great reviews from my friends and I understood that I should give it a try. 

Now when I finished the game and I am sitting here writing this review, I understand that it was worth it and the game brought me a lot of great moments that I will remember for a long time, that’s for sure. Ghostrunner is one of those games that seriously hooks the player and tests their skill. It has that one of the most satisfying feelings in gaming when you are frustrated, but you still want to move on, just to try it one more time and when you finally achieve it, the feeling is priceless. 

[b] Gameplay [/b]

The player takes the role of the deadly swordsman wearing katana, who finds himself being thrown on the dumpster. He doesn’t remember a thing about himself and his story, but he always hears the mysterious voice in his head of a man called The Architect, who takes the role of his guide in this cruel world. 

Ghostrunner is a really fast game filled with neverending action and perfectly designed levels, where every single enemy is a serious threat because this game has “one shot-one kill” mechanics. This kind of mechanics leads to pretty tricky combat where the player has to replay one level, again and again, to get through it. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2275704488

There is one and the only weapon in this game - a katana that can slice enemies with the speed of light. The protagonist can run on the walls, stick to certain points to get to the needed location, ride on the ziplines. The main trick of the game is to make a combo of all these actions that end up with a sword slice to kill the enemies. Sometimes it can be tricky and difficult but once you get the idea of how it works, the game will start to shine for you.

Ghostrunner starts with pretty easy and basic enemies that shoot you with a pistol and they are not that big of a problem to deal with. Once I got into the game and learned how to kill them all in the most efficient way, the game started to throw me much harder enemies such as gun turrets and enemies with a shield that can only be killed from behind. Enemies are getting harder and more tricky the more you progress with the game and this is the normal thing in general. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2275704585

The best part of the game is that it never lets the player feel bored or exhausted, the whole experience always keeps the player in a good shape by giving them tricky levels to get through and a reasonable amount of enemies to overcome. However, my biggest problem with the game was that it can be a bit inconsistent with the difficulty curve. That means that I could be stuck in one level for 20 minutes, trying to solve the platforming puzzle while outsmarting the enemies, only to find out that the next one hour of the game would be pretty easy with no challenge at all. 

The player can also upgrade the protagonist using a pretty unusual method: it is presented as tetris-like figures that you have to put on the grid. The space is limited so the player has to really think which upgrade is really worth it to be put on the grid because the better the upgrade is - the more space it requires. 

From time to time, the player will be sent to a special place by the Architect to learn new skills. Those places are usually presented as a training scene where the player can instantly practice the new ability for a better understanding of how the ability works.  

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2275704679

Despite being a pretty amazing game with fast-paced action and satisfying gameplay, I can’t say that Ghostrunner has great bosses to be proud of. It has three bosses in total and they are all completely unremarkable and easy to beat. Well okay, maybe I am lying - the first one was a bit challenging, but still not something that I will be remembering for a long time. 

The weakest part of the game is definitely its story. I always had a feeling like “I saw this somewhere already” or “I heard this kind of a dialogue before” or “this plot twist is something that has been experienced already a lot of times before”, etc. And when it came to the end of the game, I was sitting with a complete stone face thinking “Yeah, yeah, whatever. I will pretend that I am extremely surprised”.    

[b] Graphics [/b]

Ghostrunner doesn’t make a revolution in terms of graphics but it looks amazing most of the time. You should keep in mind that the ray-tracing option is not optimized at all, it seriously affects the framerate, but what’s more important is that it almost doesn’t make any difference to the game when it’s turned on.

[b] Sound [/b] 

The music in Ghostrunner is outstanding and if you love synthwave music, I have some pretty great news for you. [h1][b]Runner's High…[/b][/h1]
» There is no shortage of great ninja-centric video games out there, from Metal Gear Rising to more recent gems like Katana Zero. But even among those, [b]Ghostrunner[/b] stands out by being 100% committed to delivering that fantasy of becoming a super fast and deadly assassin. This is a game where you run fast, slide fast, kill fast, and if you can’t do those things fast enough, you die fast. It can be very demanding and requires pinpoint platforming precision and split-second decision-making, but it’s rarely ever frustrating thanks to instant respawns, mostly generous checkpointing, and most importantly, open-ended combat encounters that offer multiple methods of approach.

[h1]Environment[/h1]
» Taking place in a cyberpunk-themed post-apocalypse, Ghostrunner tells the story of a cybernetically enhanced swordsman who awakens after getting thrown out of a tower with little memory of what happened to him, who he is, or why he feels compelled to immediately plunge a sword into the poor soul waiting below him. Guided by the disembodied voice of an old man known as The Architect, the Ghostrunner gets wrapped up in an ongoing power struggle between the supposed rulers of this broken world, the efforts of a dying resistance, and the mystery of who he is.

[h1]Story[/h1]
» It’s a predictable tale, but the story is nonetheless well told and respectably voice-acted. What’s especially great though is how the storytelling rarely slows down the fast pace of this six to eight-hour campaign. There’s a lot of well-acted dialogue in Ghostrunner, but it all plays out via conversations that happen in the head of the main character. That gives you the choice to either stop and listen intently to what’s being said or to just push on through the various parkour-heavy platforming challenges that typically accompany any long exposition dumps.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
» Of course, the action is what you’re here for – and if you’ve got a thing for lightning-quick, reflex-intensive, high-risk/high-reward combat that gets decided with just a single strike, then Ghostrunner was made just for you.

The only main weapon in Ghostrunner is a sword, though your speed and mobility options are weapons unto themselves. The Ghostrunner can run along walls, slide down slopes with great speed, and also utilize a quick dash that can be held down to slow down time and alter the direction of his momentum in mid-air. Chaining all of these abilities together created a wonderful flow of movement that allowed me to nearly effortlessly close the distance between me and the more basic enemies before satisfyingly slicing them in half.

[h1]Combat[/h1]
» Those basic enemies aren’t your only foes for long though, and one of the best things about Ghostrunner is how your adversaries always rise to meet your growing skills and abilities. Just when I got comfortable dodging and deflecting the bullets of the single-shot pistol-wielding enemies, I had to deal with machine gun-wielding soldiers who forced me to keep moving if I wanted to survive long enough to be able to hit them while they were reloading. After I got used to dealing with those, I had to learn how to deal with shielded enemies that could only be hit from behind.

Ghostrunner does an amazing job of always keeping its action fresh, and not just by periodically adding in new enemy types. Pretty much every level introduces something new into the mix, whether it’s an environmental mechanic like grind rails that completely change up how you navigate through a level, a temporary powerup such as a slow down that allows you to deal with a group of enemies that would otherwise be nearly impossible to take on without dying or a shield battery that must be destroyed first to deal with the rest of the enemies in an encounter. Ghostrunner rarely stays on one theme for too long, and as a result, the combat feels impeccably paced and never feels like it's running out of ideas.

Best of all is the amount of flexibility each combat scenario offers. There are often multiple entry points to any given encounter and each comes with its challenges. You might take the right side and have to deal with a machine gun enemy and a long path before you can get to him. Or you could take the left path, take down a ninja guarding a shuriken powerup, and then grind on a rail sniping enemies as you go. I felt like I was always rewarded for checking out different routes whenever I hit a wall.

[h1]Platforming[/h1]
» While its platforming portions are much more linear, they still benefit from a ton of variety in their challenges. Sometimes you’ll have to hack something to freeze it in place while you navigate through or around it, other times you’ll have to quickly throw shurikens at power plates to open a door and dash through it before it closes, and you’ll often find yourself using dash in creative ways to get through tricky obstacles. The deep well of ideas Ghostrunner uses to power its short campaign is not quite Titanfall 2 levels, but it’s extremely deep nonetheless.

However, sometimes these ideas do overreach a bit and don’t quite fit with Ghostrunner’s controls. One section, for example, has you collecting 13 items scattered all around a constantly rotating object. It’s an awkward area with physics that feels off and frustrating mantling issues that send you flying towards your death when all you meant to do was pull yourself up to a ledge.

[h1]Upgrading[/h1]
» Ghostrunner also uses an interesting, albeit slightly gimmicky, upgrade system that allows you to alter and enhance your abilities. You earn upgrades automatically as you progress, which take the form of Tetris-like blocks that can be rotated and placed onto a grid. Space is limited, and the better upgrades take much more of the grid, so you’ll have to pick and choose which upgrades you want to have active at any time. The upgrades themselves are pretty good, and I found myself largely keeping space reserved for deflection-based options since I loved being able to bounce bullets back at enemies. That said, I found myself not caring about rearranging puzzle pieces to try and find an “optimal” placement, especially since any unused spaces on the grid will speed up your regeneration of a resource called focus.

Focus can be used to power one of your four special moves that function as a limited and situationally dependent ace in the hole. Blink, for example, can cut straight through shielded and otherwise tough to bring down enemies with one strike and keep your momentum going; Tempest, on the other hand, can be used to reflect projectiles that are otherwise extremely tough to avoid; and Surge is an anime-style sword energy slash that can take out multiple enemies from a distance. The last special move is a bit of a spoiler, but also has its situational advantages.

It’s also impressive that Ghostrunner’s sights and sounds are no slouch either. This is a gorgeous-looking game with an equally excellent synthwave-inspired soundtrack that will keep your head bumping throughout.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
» With its breakneck pace and skill-heavy gameplay, Ghostrunner is a speedrunner’s dream. But even beyond that demographic, this is a great first-person action game that feels punishing but fair. You may die hundreds of times, but instantaneous respawns and generous checkpointing ensure that Ghostrunner’s challenging combat and platforming never become a chore. More than all of that though, Ghostrunner is jam-packed with a great variety of enemies, mechanics, and special powers that constantly changed up how I approached its many unique encounters. That meant it always felt fresh, and by the end of its six to eight-hour campaign, I was all too eager to jump back in for seconds.

[h1][b]Score: 8.6/10[/b][/h1]

I wasn't sure if I would like Ghostrunner when I first started playing. Many mechanics felt unusual and took some getting used to, but I pushed through and discovered one of my favorite games of the past few years. I wound up beating the base game in around 8 hours and went back through to collect missing achievements. I then bought the DLC and did the same thing, totaling around 18 hours for 100% completion. Reflecting on it now, I wanted to share my experiences with the gameplay of Ghostrunner and why you should play it if you haven’t already.

My initial struggle with Ghostrunner came from its most basic element - the one-hit death mechanic. It is impossible to Google or read about this game without finding complaints about this, and my initial frustration with the mechanic was similar to what I saw online. In the end, I wound up embracing this as one of the keys to making the game so fast-paced and exciting. Nothing forces a player to stay on the move or kill enemies quickly like the threat of being killed by a single stray bullet or beam. Even though the deaths were frustrating, they provided me with the opportunity to learn areas, better predict enemy movement and attacks, and make me better at the game through repetition. The sense of satisfaction from overcoming these challenges was also high. Nothing feels better than finally clearing a very challenging level or phase, and this game is able to deliver that feeling with almost every area. Because the one-hit mechanic is permanent, the stakes remain high even if you revisit earlier levels once beating the game. You may have new equipment to tackle an arena in a creative new way, but nothing will prevent you from getting killed if you’re careless. Constant intensity is a difficult element for games to pull off, but this game achieves it with one-hit death and a variety of other gameplay features.

In addition to one-hit, this game stays intense and engaging through pace. Movement, abilities, enemy attacks, and environmental hazards are all fast-paced and designed to keep a player on their toes. The introduction of new abilities and mechanics is evenly paired with the addition of more challenging enemies and level scenarios. For example, an upgrade to be able to reflect enemy projectiles more easily is useful against standard guards, but is much more difficult to use against guards with automatic weapons. Every ability feels like it has an enemy or scenario to balance it out, and vice versa. The upgrade system feels extremely balanced, never making things too easy for you, but able to give you an edge if you build your upgrades around a playstyle that works for you. The combination of ability unlocks, level secrets, and challenging and fast-paced gameplay all amount to a genuine feeling of progression when moving to a new level, equipping a new buff, or even finding a new sword cosmetic to use. Of course, all this progression needs an equally dynamic soundtrack.

The soundtrack for Ghostrunner caught me by surprise. Intense, engaging tracks perfectly match the feelings of speed and power from mowing through enemies and exploring a post-apocalyptic indoor city. Daniel Deluxe made the soundtrack for both the base game and the Project Hel DLC, and I can’t recommend his work enough. I often find myself listening to the soundtracks and his other albums while driving, working, or jogging. In short, the music for Ghostrunner perfectly matches and contributes to the aesthetic and pace of the game, all while making the experience feel much more whole and cinematic. With all of this said, there is still room for criticism.

Ghostrunner is an excellent game in my opinion, but that doesn’t mean there isn’t room for improvement. The saving system is fairly basic, only saving progress after a level is completed, with no level checkpoints or other means of saving progress partway through. While this wasn’t a huge issue for me personally, I could see how someone more strapped for time to play might be frustrated by having to redo a level they finished most of but didn’t complete. Another minor issue I noticed was the lack of colorblind options. I am colorblind and found distinguishing between certain subtle shades to be challenging, especially during the cybervoid sequences. With that said, this wasn’t too much of a hindrance and I was able to play the game as normal, but this is something that would be nice to have. While I didn’t take much issue with it, another criticism I’ve seen echoed online is the overall difficulty of this game, either due to one-shot deaths or a random enemy attack that seems to come out of nowhere. After having completed everything the game has to offer, I would make the same argument here that I did in my death stranding review. In that review, I said:

“The current landscape of gaming is a sharp juxtaposition to the focus of this game. Instant gratification in the forms of seamless matchmaking, easy to learn controls, dynamic difficulty settings, and much more all contribute to a culture where people expect and demand a seamless experience. Many games are beatable with minimal experience or understanding of mechanics either because they are similar to other titles, or because developers have opted to make the game as welcoming as possible for a more diverse audience. While there isn't anything wrong with any of this, Death Stranding simply is not one of these games.”

I feel that this sentiment largely applies to Ghostrunner as well. In my experience, the game didn’t feel at all unfair or unbalanced, but it definitely wasn’t accommodating either. A player who is not familiar with games featuring a faster pace or repetitive deaths will need to play more in order to succeed and move forward, but this definitely isn’t a bad thing. My final thought on this is - if you are looking for a game that is both challenging and satisfying, this may be for you. If you are not interested in practice-makes-perfect, you may be better off looking elsewhere. I also saw some complaints of the bosses being simplistic and mechanics being applied inconsistently but didn’t notice either of these things during my time playing. I definitely took time to learn enemy movements and the different ways enemies can react to the player’s actions, but didn’t notice anything wildly inconsistent or challenging as a result.

Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed Ghostrunner. It is one of just a few games I’ve 100% completed on steam and it’s for a reason. I had a great time playing both the base game and DLC, and loved the way they varied in mechanics and presentation. I’m definitely looking forward to future releases from 505, and hope this game gets a quality sequel that expands upon the mechanics of the game and also exposes us to more lore associated with the light, but interesting story.

I absolutely loved the environments, art direction, hidden collectible swords, and the most of the short story (despite the painfully predictable twist at the end). I Enjoyed the movement (mostly), melee combat (to an extent), and the rush of chaining together kills; losing myself in a blur of neon slashes and multicolored viscera and/or circuits. However, as I played more and more, the painfully rough patches became harder and harder to ignore. 

I felt as if the movement at it's best was simple and fairly fast, but at it's worst it was clunky, imprecise, inconsistent, and needlessly restrictive. Clambering can be an absolute life-ender when an enemy is positioned on the edge of a platform you're all too likely to clamber onto. Clambering also will force you forward, so if you wanted to just climb on top of a crate odds are it'll vault you with mild speed well past it. Also the game introduces a grapple mechanic past the first level and at what range you will be able to use it is functioning entirely on a case-by-case basis, sometimes barely crossing a gap you would've just been short of jumping past and sometimes allowing you to cover entire canyons with no real distinction as to how much momentum you'll be given. The game also right out the gate gives you the power to dash and later you'll be able to mod to hold multiple dash charges. The catch to such a potential mobility increase is that while in the air you can not dash more than once. A massive pet-peeve of mine was figuring out that while in air you can not quickly tap your dash key to strafe left or right, you have to enter the slow-mo mode to input such a command. Also, I just wish your base movement speed was faster in general, even after figuring out I could maintain a good speed by chaining quick slides and jumps, It just didn't quite match the kind of speed I'd expect from a fully-augmented cyberpunk samurai warrior who relies primarily on melee combat.

The enemies for the most part were fine and I enjoyed facing up against most of them, with four being more of a nuisance than a compelling threat. The first being 180 shield units, which I'll give the benefit of the doubt that fighting them hasn't quite "clicked" for me, despite my brain telling me that their shield hitboxes are larger and less forgiving than the visual would indicate. The second being lunging melee units, just because I can't play more aggressively and strike them down mid-air, trying to do so just results in death. The third is samurai units, who I again wish I could play more aggressively against; a simple change to make it so striking them first would result in an immediate counter attack (that I could then parry) would make a world of a difference. The other unit is the suicide units, which I hate on a personal level not for being a threat, but instead lacking any compelling method of dispatching them besides having an ability charged or simply running away. 

Speaking of abilities, I feel like they could've been much more compelling, but after I had unlocked all upgrades I fell onto using tempest for virtually every situation. Considering it accomplishes the jobs of both blink (excluding lunging you forward) and surge by also being a large AOE cone in front of the player that can destroy bullets, but also having an upgrade than upon killing just two enemies at once will refund the entire ability cost back. I thought overlord was interesting as well, but was much more niche in use. 

The bosses of this game are one of it's notably disappointing sections. Painfully simple, repetitive, and under-utilizing of existing mechanics at best and outright ignoring them at worst. The first boss is itself a giant pattern, the only thing separating you from a flawless completion is a memorization of it's pattern and the ability to execute on it. The second boss is the same, yet when it leaped away I felt a slight rush knowing I'll need to move quickly and evasively to reach them, only to realize they had barely covered two-wall runs worth of distance and was throwing projectiles with the speed of a cheap paper airplane. Finally, the final boss, nothing short of a repeat of the prior albeit with a bit of variance to the order of 3 attacks it would perform. There was no parkour to speak of here, save for wall running in a circle for a few seconds when the floor became dangerous. None of these bosses allow for ability use, invalidating not only the abilities but the upgrades for said abilities as well. 

The absolute lowest point goes to the cyberspace sequences, pulling you from your fast-paced hack/slash experience to throw you in an untextured grid space to solve puzzles no more complex than connect the dots. Even worse is when it requires you to do platforming without wall-run, dashes, or even sprint. I was fortunate enough to know about bunny hopping by the time I reached those challenges, but outside of moving through empty hallways faster, they became useless all over again when I realized the platforms were spaced to just accommodate a walking-pace platformer.

I've collected all misc items and all swords, I am in the process of building up the patience to return and complete the hardcore added a few months ago, and am still looking forward to upcoming DLC for the game. However, I can only hope a host of changes come to improve base gameplay alongside such updates, else I'll be putting off all future purchases until a very generous discount comes around.

Ghostrunner is a super punishing trial and error game in the same vein as Hotline Miami and Super Meat Boy. Wall run, dash, slide and cut robot men up with your trusty katana but just don't take a hit, because you go down faster than 2nd grade Algebra. It's a frustrating learning curve to come to grips with but becomes really satisfying once you break through it and start kicking ass. Just be prepared, you're gonna die a lot.

Full video review:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7tDFf4QUGWM

To describe this game in a word: [i] inconsistency [/i].
At its best, Ghostrunner feels slick, fast, and badass. You build momentum, cut through enemies in one hit, and pull off some wicked cool moves. You really feel like a superhuman killing machine.

However, most of your time in this game will be spent dying to poor platforming mechanics, enemies you can't even hope to see, and spotty inputs that leave you extremely vulnerable. The platforming only works about half the time; I can't tell you how often I just ran straight off the top of a wall because I started the wall run just barely higher than I meant to. I also can't tell you how many times the AI did completely different things in response to the same action. And I frequently missed point-blank attacks that left me completely open to getting shot.

This was one of my most anticipated games of the holiday season. Unfortunately, I feel like it needed a few more months of work. If it was a little more polished, if a few annoying mechanics were tweaked a bit, if the developers just took a little longer to really make the game shine, this could have been a masterpiece. I still think it could be a masterpiece; if the developers can patch out some of the issues (primarily the platforming physics and input problems), I will gladly change my review to an emphatic recommendation.

The game is best described as cyberpunk Mirror's Edge with a bit of combat. The levels are linear, and the main focus is on the parkour/platforming. There's a generic sci-fi story going on in the background, but you can't make any choices that affect it. You die in one hit, so the game is more about trying the same section over and over again, sometimes with very precise timing, until you can do it perfectly, rather than improvising solutions.

The parkour is good. It feels fast and the controls are nice and smooth, once you get the hang of them at least. Flying through the air dodging bullets and then landing on a guy and chopping him in half is really fun, even when you have to repeat it exactly the same 30 times in a row. I do wish, though, that you had a few more moves. Here you basically just have wall run, slide, dash, and a grappling hook to pre-determined points. Mirror's Edge also had vaulting, swinging, vertical wall runs, balance beams and probably some other stuff I'm forgetting, and that game wasn't even sci-fi. What's there is fun but they could have added a lot more.

Combat really feels like another platforming challenge with some added pressure, rather than a fight. Since you die in one hit, and most enemies don't move, a combat encounter is basically just figuring out the optimal way to move through the environment and kill everything, and then trying again and again until you get it right. If you hide behind a box, you can wait there as long as you like to figure out your next move. There are a couple of special moves you unlock which kill enemies from a bit further away, but they have a very long cooldown so you can only really use one per encounter, and they end up feeling more like 'get out of jail free cards' in case you find one section too difficult, rather than proper weapons you would use on the fly. Most of the time I forgot they existed.

Just to drive home the fact that the game is not about combat, the final boss of the game isn't even a boss, it's just an extra-difficult platforming section with no enemies.

The environments all look good, but none are particularly memorable, and something about the way everything is composed of these very large, sometimes nonsensical platforms makes them start to feel like they're not really real places, just testbeds made by a game designer. By the end of the game (about 8 hours), I was pretty sick of being in them.

I definitely recommend using mouse + keyboard. To do certain moves you need to flick your mouse around quite precisely and I have no idea how you'd do it with a controller. Low framerate also makes the game a lot harder - I had to stop streaming and lower the graphics a bit just to make combat playable (I have a GTX 970).

Overall, I'd give it 3/5: an enjoyable 8 hours if you like the cyberpunk setting or want some fast-paced action and have already played DOOM Eternal. Worth picking up if it's on sale.

[code]Slicing your way through a cyberpunk city with a parkouring katana-wielding cyber-ninja, Ghostrunner is a tough as nails but still fair neon-filled dream to play through [/code]

The reviewing phrase “really makes you feel like X” is – rightfully – made fun of for its overuse these days. But in the case of [i]Ghostrunner[/i], it’s actually fitting: How can I not feel like a badass cyberninja when I’m wallrunning & jumping across malfunctioning electronic billboards, slowing down time to evade bullets only to then quickly move behind the shooting enemy and finish them with a quick slash of my katana? [i]Ghostrunner[/i] immediately draws the player into its world and after just a short introduction, you’ll already pull off moves right out of an action movie.

But let’s not get ahead of ourselves here, let’s start with the basics first. [i]Ghostrunner[/i] is an “action packed hardcore FPP slasher”, as the devs describe it. This might not really tell you much though – if I were to describe it, it’s a mix between [i]Titanfall 2[/i] in terms of movement and [i]DOOM[/i] (2016) in terms of analyzing enemy encounters & coming up with a combat strategy. The notable omission here is that [i]Ghostrunner[/i] doesn’t allow the player to use any guns, unlike both aforementioned titles. While you’ll get access to a few ranged attacks later in the game, the main focus here is melee combat, using a katana.

 What does this mean in practice? [i]Ghostrunner[/i] throws both, parkour and combat challenges and you. Sometimes it’s about getting to a destination, sometimes it’s about getting rid of all enemies in order to unlock doors & get further ahead. There are a few boss fights as well, but I’ll talk about those later.

Let’s talk about the parkour first. [i]Ghostrunner[/i] is fast paced and precise, so if you expect a [i]Mirror’s Edge[/i] set in darker cyberpunk world (I did), this is not the game. Besides running, sliding and jumping, you’ll be also able to wallrun on almost any surface as well as dashing through the air. Thankfully, as you’re also able to slow down time while in the air (to evade enemy bullets), you also got some wriggle room to adjust your jumps to keep up with the pace.

Thanks to a lot of visual hints, like arrows or highlighted usable objects, the fast tempo of the game is not obstructing you from knowing where to go – or well, wallrun. I only encountered three or four instances where I was not sure where to head – but when in doubt, look for a button you might’ve to press, it might open up some new ways for you!

Surprisingly, even though I’m an avid fan of [i]Titanfall 2[/i], it took me some time to really internalize the movement options. That’s mostly thanks to the unusual control scheme of [i]Ghostrunner[/i], which used a different jumping button on my Xbox One controller (RB) than other platforming games usually use (A). However, as I kept on playing, I quickly grew fond of the controls and soon I was able to perform platforming challenges without much trouble.

The part of the game probably causing you more deaths are the enemy encounters. Starting with simple soldiers with guns, the enemy rooster quickly grows with additions such as katana wielders, robots, snipers or shielded gunners. Here’s where the similarity to [i]DOOM[/i] (2016) comes from – you’ll enter the combat arena, quickly make note of the different enemy type & their positions and then come up with a plan on the spot: which enemy do I prioritize? How can I use the arena layout to my advantage?

Of course, planning and executing said plans are two different things. But when you’re finally able to pull off everything just as you planned it to be, maybe with a bit of improvisation if needed, and get that slow-mow kill for the last enemy – what a feeling. The adrenaline rush of dodging enemy attacks and taking out high priority targets first, is only getting better thanks to the fantastic electronic soundtrack supporting every action.

Over the course of the game, [i]Ghostrunner[/i] also supplies you with upgrades and new special abilities. These are only really expanding your toolkit though; I didn’t really feel like I was “missing” anything vital even with just the basic abilities. However, being able to slice enemies from afar or dash twice turned out to be quite helpful. There are also various (optional) collectibles, like audio logs or new sword designs, hidden throughout the world – but to be honest, I was so busy/happy with making my way through the chapters at high pace, I never really wanted to stop just to look for them. 

What’s most important to note here is that, besides it’s fast pace, [i]Ghostrunner[/i] is not called “hardcore” by the devs for nothing – you’ll die. A lot. It takes just one hit or one wrong jump to be reunited with the game over screen. As the game shows you the time taken and number of deaths suffered at the end of each chapter, you’ll quickly get familiar with just how often you might die.

That said, with all the many, many deaths I’ve gotten, I rarely felt like the death wasn’t my fault. You’ll know why you got that game over and it’s mostly because of yourself – didn’t dodge a bullet, jumped too late, parried at the wrong time. I never felt like I was hitting a wall, because I always knew what I had to improve in order to get further. So even while [i]Ghostrunner[/i] is a tough game requiring a lot of try-and-error, it’s not unfair. And with a lot of automatic checkpoints, there were only one or two instances where I wished for a different checkpoint placement.

The only parts of the game that caused some minor frustrations were the boss fights, the first one in particular. I actually felt like the bosses went from harder to easier, instead of the other way around. While they are also testing your movement and combat abilities, some of the moves can be quite difficult to dodge – I personally wasn’t always able to determine just how big the hitbox of an enemy attack was. But as there are only a few boss fights in the game – with checkpoints for different phases as well – they didn’t really detract from the experience.

The only thing accompanying you through the beautifully rendered (if a bit generic) cyberpunk city besides the great OST are story dialogues. I’m mentioning this last because I feel like the game really shines mostly thanks to its movement and combat. That’s not saying the story of [i]Ghostrunner[/i] is based, it does add a lot to the atmosphere – flashing out the world and characters. However, it’s also really predictable to the point where a friend watching me friend was also able to figure out the ending from just a few dialogues.

In the end, I was able to beat [i]Ghostrunner[/i] in about 7 hours, which I feel was the perfect length for a game like it. Throughout this time, the game always threw something new at me, making me use the entirety of my toolset instead of just sticking to the same strategies. I never got bored and by the time I finished, I immediately knew I was going to buy the sequel to this one once it releases. 

Everyone who wants a fast-paced game with brilliant movement and enemy design should take a look at this game. While the story doesn’t offer anything revolutionary, the gameplay alone carries this game for me, and I simply can’t wait to play as a cyberninja again.

[h1] Gotta go fast [/h1]
Speed is something inherently connected with what “Arcade” means. Be they platformer games of old or far more modern twists on the idea, Arcade games mostly reward playing at neck-breaking speed. More points, secret level, hidden boss or an extra life. Whatever the prize may be, there is a peculiar satisfaction to be drawn from playing not only well but also really fast. This sensation is the quintessence of what Ghostrunner is – a frantic rush towards victory, an obstacle course you failed 50 times and the joy of overcoming challenge once you finally make it. An idea of frantic race against time drawn straight out of the earliest of games. All wrapped into a modern first-person action game package, flavoured with cyberpunk setting. And it did come out.

[b] Good morning, agent 74 [/b]
You are a Ghostrunner – an ultimate fusion of man and machine, capable of running on the side of the building as easily as if it was a walk down the aisle. Armed with a kick-ass katana and mind-boggling speed, you are a peacekeeper and arbitrator, one of the hundred. The last one. Once, your kind protected the Dharma Tower, a megastructure built to house what remains of humanity. As for the outside? Enough time have passed since the cataclysm, that the existence of great outdoors is a leap of logic rather than something anyone would be familiar with. 

Your story ended when the rulers of the tower decided to struggle for power. Ghostrunners rushed to their master’s aid, too bad the cybernetic implants that gave them their power were undone by a simple click on the “off” button.  Unit 74 was cast down from the high spires all the way to the lowest industrial levels but not killed. Pile of spare parts, some duct tape, sheer luck and a band of underspire rebels later – Ghostrunner is reborn mere 20 years after the fall. Armed with a new nanoblade and guided by another echo from the past you undertake a journey, both proverbial and literal, back to the very top of Dharma Tower. You have a score to settle with the new management and the killswitch won’t work this time.
[url] https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2304716838 [/url]
[b] Dodge the bullets [/b]
Frankly, story of this title is little more than a pretence to keep the player going and it meets that end with decency. A cherry on top, if you may. However, Ghostrunner is first and foremost about  the gameplay loop and it is a glorious one. No further incentive to cut the baddies to ribbons is necessary, other than simply witnessing how fun it is. Combat is built around simple principle, any enemy can be cut down in a single hit and so can you. The adversaries compose of steadily increasing gallery of cybernetically augmented thugs. While the enemy bionics are nowhere nearly as good as yours, they do have the numbers, guns and better positions. All futile, because they didn’t bring a restart button and you did. Checkpoint-based save system of Ghostrunner is worked into the game with such an exceptional fluidity that at times, you may not even notice the death as 74 jumps right back into the fray.

Each level can be broken down into a set of arenas, many among them designed specifically to highlight the latest addition to the enemy roster. Given that Ghostrunner takes about 6 hours to beat the selection is surprisingly wide. Slowly charging guns quickly receive backup equipped with automated rifles, then melee specialists, attack drones and far more outlandish foes. Once you get the hang of it, each skirmish becomes a puzzle with multiple correct solutions. To somewhat even the odds, with progress the player receives their own powers. A forward dash capable of cutting even the bullets or a blade-shaped surge of energy slicing enemies from a distance. More interestingly, any unlocked power stays with the player for the replay of any completed level. Think you can best your first level completion time with one of the late-game abilities? Go ahead and try.

[b] Improvise. Adapt. Overrun. [/b]
Next to combat, the second pillar Ghostrunner is built upon would be parkour. As a primary way of keeping the low profile during his climb, 74 takes a scenic route wherever possible. In practice, between each combat section there is a cyberpunk-themed parkour obstacle course with environmental hazards instead of a safety net. Every step of the way requires good timing, a lot of wall running, mid-air dashes and most importantly – a neck-breaking pace. Each level contains a number of visual hints pointing in the right direction, to allow fluid progress even on the first playthrough. It is extremely important to keep the proper tempo, as often simply loosing the rhythm is enough to get the player killed. The entire game is a merciless challenge that seems impossible to complete at the first glance, only to become a piece of cake with enough practice.

Ghostrunner continuously blends together acrobatics and brutal melee into a blissful adrenaline rush. Completing a level often feels like finishing the craziest amusement park ride you’ve ever been to. Once you catch a breath you can’t help but crave another go, just for the thrill of it. Furthermore, this title constantly introduces new elements and switches the environment to prevent the game from ever becoming stale. The second you get used to lower-level industrial interiors, the game introduces the cybervoid – a realm of cybernetic blackness and neon, where protagonist’s mind travels to solve logic puzzles and learn new powers. Soon thereafter, unit 74 reaches living hubs and then the high spires, each visually different from the previous one.

The game naturally challenges player to beat each level as fast as possible. Ghostrunner always records time and death count, inviting the player to improve their previous score. If any of your friends on Steam also played the game, you have their times displayed during level summary. 

[b] Critical failure [/b]
However sweet Ghostrunner may be, the game is hardly all milk and honey. Despite creators seemingly addressing the issue with every patch – Ghostrunner has a considerable amount of collision detection issues, especially for a game about threading the needle. For the most part, none of such kinks appear consistently, then again seeing your record-breaking attempt squandered by falling through the wall you easily leapt off in previous 20 runs is mighty frustrating. This is by far the biggest problem of the game, which doesn’t mean other minor bugs don’t occasionally occur. The weirdest one during my playtime forbid me from using my sword after deflecting a bullet. Nothing but restarting the game helped. Underused enemies from later stages of the game are a slightly different matter. There is so much happening later on, that Splitter or Mirage enemies seem to get nowhere nearly the attention other adversaries had. Instead we get a good solid look at the irritating suicide bombers – an enemy type that often forces the player to break otherwise fluid running rhythm of the game. 

Ultimately, I consider Ghostrunner to be a modern incarnation of old arcade games at heart. Despite small flaws, the game is ridiculously fun to play, although it heavily relies on the player to meet a single condition – this is a game for thrill-seekers. If you find satisfaction in repeatedly overcoming challenges then this title easily becomes a must-play. Those among you with more laid-back approach to gaming are likely to find the experience rather vexing. To everyone else, Ghostrunner is highly recommendable top-quality piece of action. In my book, this title is easily one of the best releases of 2020 and as a cherry on top - it comes at a modest price.

This amazing parkour/ninja-style game has gorgeous graphics, fantastic music and an uninterrupted gameplay experience with no useless cutscenes. The essence of the game can be likened to an intricate puzzle, where death is your faithful companion until you discover the optimal path to conquer every enemy encounter. (similar to Geometry Dash)

What sets this game apart is the inclusion of a "restart" button, a brilliant addition that eliminates loading times and allows you to restart from the checkpoint if you know that you are going to die. Additionally, the game features 2-3 normal puzzles that surpass the quality of those found in the Resident Evil 3 Remake. I love that the upgrading system follows a Tetris-like style.

The game has 2 extra gamemodes:
1) Kill Run: Race against the clock while killing enemies and collecting "time" items. This mode is designed for those who want to challenge their skills.
2) Wave Mode (a true gem): After completing each wave, you can unlock random active / passive skills, as well as modifiers. For example, you can find ways to defeat enemies by bypassing their shields or gain a shield that lets you take 1 more hit before dying. This feature significantly amplifies replay value (since every playthrough is different) and is a valuable tool for skill improvement.

However, I do have a couple of complaints. 
The first boss battle is a bad experience; it is very frustrating as there is so much shit that you need more luck than anything (and dying with one single hit does not help). 
The final parkour section presents quite a challenge and it might have been wiser to preserve this level of difficulty for an extra game mode, where the focus is solely on completing the parkour course as fast as possible. 

In conclusion, I absolutely recommend this game but be aware that you are going to die 40 - 100 times per level. 
It's defitenely a challenge but an amazing experience.
